In construction, buildings are made from prefabricated parts (walls, windows, beams and so

Each part is self-contained.

But software doesn’t stay simple forever. As we add new features, fix 
bugs, and respond to changing needs.
Lehman’s Laws
Meir M. Lehman, a pioneer in software engineering, observed how large software systems 
behave over time. 
These are scientific laws — they describe how things behave, not how they should be.
Two Key Laws:
Law of Increasing Complexity: 
Every time we make changes to the program, it becomes a bit more complicated, 
unless we clean it up.
Law of Continuing Change: 
If a program is useful, people will want it to do more over time. 
So, it needs to keep changing to stay useful.

Key Modularity Principles
How do we manage this growing complexity? One of the most effective 
tools we have is modular design.
High Cohesion: Each module does one clear task.
Low Coupling: Modules don’t overly depend on each other.
Information Hiding: A module hides its internal details and exposes only 
what others need.
Code Reuse: Shared functionality should be in one place and reused.

Easier to Understand: Focus on one small part at a time.
Easier to Test: Test each part by itself.
Easier to Change: Modify one module without breaking others.
Encourages Reuse: use the same module where needed.
Benefits of Modularity

Splitting up modules.
Combining separate modules into one.
Moving parts of one module into another.

Software Maintenance
What Is the Problem?

The final stage of the software lifecycle.

Begins after delivery or release.

Unlike hardware, software doesn’t wear out — issues are usually pre-existing.
For example,
You release a web app in 2002. Everything seems fine.
In 2025, a user enters an unusual name with special characters, and the app crashes. 
The crash didn’t happen because the software “wore out.”
The software always had a hidden bug that wasn’t triggered before.
With modular design:
Fix small parts without breaking the whole system (corrective)
Enhance features more easily (perfective)
Swap or update components for new environments (adaptive)

Coupling – Interdependence Between Modules
e.g. In a date-handling module:
isLeapYear(y) determine whether the year is a leap year.
calcDaysInMonth(m,y) calculate the number of days in a given month and year
To correctly compute the days in February, calcDaysInMonth(m,y) must determine 
whether the year is a leap year.
calcDaysInMonth(m,y) calls isLeapYear(y) to ﬁnd out.
Thus, calcDaysInMonth(m,y) depends on isLeapYear(y)
This kind of dependency is called coupling.
Note : Coupling can result from both interactions between modules and the way parameters 
are used.

Degree of Coupling
Coupling varies in strength:
Loose coupling (preferred)
Tight coupling (problematic)
We prefer it to be as loose as possible:
The loosest coupling is not no coupling.
Some coupling is essential for functionality.
Problems with tight coupling:
Changes in one module strongly affect another.
Developers must understand both modules simultaneously.
Aim for loose coupling to improve modularity, maintainability, and scalability.

Things to consider : Calls
A function call (also known as an invocation) is the most direct and visible form of coupling.
What happens during a call:
1. when calcDaysInMonth(m,y) calls isLeapYear(y):
2. calcDaysInMonth pauses execution.
3. The value y(year) is passed to isLeapYear(y).
4. isLeapYear performs its logic and return a result.
5. The result is returned back to calcDaysInMonth(m,y).
6. calcDaysInMonth resumes, receiving and using the result in its own computation.
The caller depends on the callee’s interface and behaviour.
Calls commonly use parameter passing and return values.

Lazy programmers use global variables as a short-cut.
“How can data get from doThingA() to doThingB()?”
“Ah ha! A global variable!”
Yes, it works,  but you will live to regret it.
def square():
  global x
  global xSquared 
    xSquared = x * x
def outputResult(): 
  global xSquared 
  print(xSquared)
if name == “__main__”:
  x = int(input()) 
  square() 
  outputResult()
Python
Input a number and stores in global variable x.
The square() function reads x, computes x*x and stores it 
in another global variable xSquared.
The outputResult() function prints xSquared.
Functions are tied together via global variables.
You can’t tell what the function uses or needs.
Easy to accidentally break as all functions share variables

Discussion
Problems with Global Variables
Changes affect everything: even unrelated parts.
Hidden connections: functions silently depend on shared data.
Hard to trace bugs: one function breaks because another changed the same variable.
Better Practice:
Pass values directly between functions. 
keep data flow explicit and clear.

Global variables can be eliminated by:
Using Parameters: when the function needs to read the variable.
Returning Values: when the function modifies and outputs the variable.
Both: when the function reads and modifies the variable.

Cohesion
Cohesion: How focused a single module is.
Think within a module/function/class.
High cohesion: the module does one job well.
Low cohesion: the module does many unrelated jobs.
High cohesion leads to more eﬃcient use of your mental resources.

Good software design has loose coupling and high cohesion.
Loose coupling: modules don’t depend on each other much.
High cohesion: each module has a clear, focused responsibility.

Improving one often improves the other:
Breaking a large, messy module with low cohesion into smaller, focused modules 
increases cohesion. These focused modules require fewer connections, which leads 
to lower coupling.
When you reduce dependencies between modules (i.e., reduce coupling), you 
naturally give each module more independence, resulting in higher cohesion.

Coupling
Focus on interactions between modules.
Function A calls B, C, D  high coupling.
Function A works independently  Low coupling.

Things to consider: Relatedness of Tasks
Even when a function does multiple tasks, the degree of cohesion depends on how related those tasks are.
Completely unrelated 
Tasks have no logical connection. Should be split entirely.
extremely low (essentially zero) cohesion.
Superficially related (e.g., by name)
Grouped under a broad label, but not functionally coherent.
low cohesion
Related by time 
Tasks must happen together or in sequence but are distinct.
Moderate Cohesion
Related by data
Tasks use or transform the same data. 
Often tightly coupled.
Higher Cohesion

Code redundancy:
Code is redundant if it performs a task that is already handled elsewhere.
Also known as: Repetition, Duplication.
Good software design aims to eliminate redundancy:
Software does not wear out — there's no benefit in duplicating logic.
Redundancy in code: Makes the program harder to maintain
Software Design
Modularity & Maintenance

Redundancy (or Repetition or Duplication)
Software and Hardware Redundancy:
Software: 
Software doesn’t wear out.
Redundancy is typically harmful.
Adds complexity without benefit.
Hardware: 
Physical components
Physical parts wear out
redundancy improves reliability. 
Backup fans, disks, etc.

Code redundancy is bad
Problems with Redundancy in Software
Increases system size unnecessarily.
Harder to test, inspect, and maintain.
Introduces risk of inconsistent behaviour.

Minimize repetition — don’t eliminate it completely
Avoid unnecessary duplication, but don’t sacrifice clarity or simplicity just to remove all repetition.
Not all repetition is bad — if it makes your code easier to read, understand, and maintain, it’s worth it.

Reuse and Coupling
Reuse is desirable…
But reuse can increase coupling, because multiple parts now depend on the same component.
Reuse and coupling are not opposites, they must be carefully balanced, not blindly optimized.
Sensible Design
Reuse only when tasks are truly the same.
Don’t “force” reuse for things that aren’t actually shared responsibilities.
Avoid introducing tight dependencies just for the sake of reuse.
If You’re Not Careful
introduce unnecessary coupling.
mistake similar-looking code for actual duplication.
reduce cohesion by forcing unrelated code to share logic.

Summary
Modularity breaks software into self-contained units (functions, classes, packages) to simplify software development.
As software evolves, complexity increases (Lehman’s Laws). Modular design helps manage this growth.
Refactoring improves internal structure without changing behaviour.
Coupling measures how tightly modules depend on each other. Aim for low coupling (independent modules).
Cohesion measures how focused a module is. Aim for high cohesion (each module does one well-defined task).
Reuse is desirable but must be balanced — it can increase coupling if not applied carefully.
